claim: Odor perception starts with odorant molecules binding to olfactory receptors.
source: Odor perception starts with odorant molecules binding to olfactory receptors.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the olfactory system.

claim: Different odorants bind to a unique set of possibly overlapping olfactory receptors.
source: Different odorants bind to a unique set of possibly overlapping olfactory receptors.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about olfactory receptor binding patterns.

claim: In rodents, each olfactory sensory neuron expresses one olfactory sensory receptor and projects to one glomerulus.
source: In rodents, each olfactory sensory neuron expresses one olfactory sensory receptor and projects to one glomerulus (Mombaerts, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Mombaerts, 2006.

claim: Each odorant activates a unique set of glomeruli, which in turn activate the olfactory bulb output neurons – the mitral and tufted (M/T) cells.
source: Each odorant activates a unique set of glomeruli, which in turn activate the olfactory bulb (OB) output neurons – the mitral and tufted (M/T) cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge about olfactory system organization.

claim: Odors are encoded by a combinatorial code composed of the set of glomeruli activated by each odor, termed the spatial code or identity code.
source: These findings led to the hypothesis that odors are encoded by a combinatorial code composed of the set of glomeruli activated by each odor. This code was termed the spatial code or identity code (Friedrich and Korsching, 1997; Friedrich and Korsching, 1998; Galizia et al., 1999; Johnson and Leon, 2007; Malnic et al., 1999; Rubin and Katz, 1999; Uchida et al., 2000).
evidence: This hypothesis is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The spatial coding scheme is theoretically capable of encoding any number of odors owing to the large number of different glomeruli.
source: Owing to the large number of different glomeruli, this coding scheme is theoretically capable of encoding any number of odors (Koulakov et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Koulakov et al., 2007.

claim: Odor stimulation evokes odor- and cell-specific temporal patterns of activity in the OB and antennal lobe, which are not directly related to the dynamics of the olfactory stimulus.
source: It has long been observed that odor stimulation evokes odor- and cell-specific temporal patterns of activity in the OB and antennal lobe, which are not directly related to the dynamics of the olfactory stimulus.
evidence: This is presented as an established observation in the field.

claim: According to the Hopfield model, odors are encoded by the identity of the odor-activated neurons and their time of activation in relation to some oscillatory cycle.
source: According to the Hopfield model, odors are encoded by the identity of the odor-activated neurons and their time of activation in relation to some oscillatory cycle (Figure 1A) (Hopfield, 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hopfield, 1995 and reference to Figure 1A.

claim: The Hopfield model provides a simple mechanism for concentration-invariant odor recognition: when the odor concentration changes, multiple neurons shift their spike timing together, such that the relative timing across neurons remains unchanged.
source: This coding model provides a simple mechanism for concentration-invariant odor recognition: when the odor concentration changes, multiple neurons shift their spike timing together, such that the relative timing across neurons remains unchanged.
evidence: This is a description of a theoretical mechanism from the Hopfield model.

claim: According to the Hopfield model, two odors that activate a similar set of glomeruli but at different times should evoke two distinguishable percepts.
source: According to this model, time is part of the odor code and therefore two odors that activate a similar set of glomeruli but at different times should evoke two distinguishable percepts.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the Hopfield model's premise that time is part of the odor code.

claim: In rodents, the latency of glomerular activation showed stimulus-specific temporal patterns.
source: In rodents, the latency of glomerular activation showed stimulus-specific temporal patterns (Spors, 2006; Spors and Grinvald, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Spors, 2006 and Spors and Grinvald, 2002.

claim: Increasing the odor concentration reduced the glomeruli onset times while preserving the temporal sequence of glomerular activation.
source: Moreover, increasing the odor concentration reduced the glomeruli onset times while preserving the temporal sequence of glomerular activation, suggesting that the temporal sequence of glomeruli activation encodes the odor identity, whereas the time of activation encodes concentration (Spors and Grinvald, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Spors and Grinvald, 2002.

claim: In larvae of Xenopus laevis, latency from stimulus onset across M/T cells reliably conveyed stimulus information about odor identity and concentration.
source: In larvae of Xenopus laveis (a model organism that does not sniff), latency from stimulus onset across M/T cells reliably conveyed stimulus information about odor identity and concentration (Junek et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Junek et al., 2010.

claim: Downstream neurons in mice are sensitive to the relative activation times of optogenetically activated output neurons in the olfactory bulb.
source: Consistent with latency coding, a study reported that downstream neurons in mice are sensitive to the relative activation times of optogenetically activated output neurons in the olfactory bulb (Haddad et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Haddad et al., 2013.

claim: Mice are able to discriminate between optogenetic stimulations of olfactory neurons, which differ mainly in their activation times, either relative to the sniff cycle or to each other.
source: Finally, several behavioral studies have shown that mice are able to discriminate between optogenetic stimulations of olfactory neurons, which differ mainly in their activation times, either relative to the sniff cycle or to each other (Rebello et al., 2014; Smear et al., 2011; Smear et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Rebello et al., 2014; Smear et al., 2011; Smear et al., 2013.

claim: Odors are encoded by the early components of the activated glomeruli, whereas the components activated later could possibly be utilized to differentiate between highly similar odors.
source: A more recent variant of the latency model suggested that odors are encoded by the early components of the activated glomeruli (Schaefer and Margrie, 2007; Wilson et al., 2017), whereas the components activated later in the evolving spatiotemporal map could possibly be utilized to differentiate between highly similar odors (Schaefer and Margrie, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Schaefer and Margrie, 2007 and Wilson et al., 2017.

claim: Neurons in the piriform cortex tend to respond to the early components and ignore the later ones.
source: Consistent with this model, a recent study showed that neurons in the piriform cortex tend to respond to the early components and ignore the later ones (Bolding and Franks, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bolding and Franks, 2018.

claim: According to the Laurent model, populations of neurons exhibit synchronized oscillatory activity, but each neuron only transiently participates in this population activity.
source: The Laurent model, by contrast, stresses that populations of neurons exhibit synchronized oscillatory activity, but that each neuron only transiently participates in this population activity (Laurent, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Laurent, 2002.

claim: The identities of neurons that participate in the oscillatory ensemble change over time and form the odor representation that is gradually decorrelated to improve odor encoding in neural space.
source: The identities of neurons that participate in the oscillatory ensemble change over time and form the odor representation that is gradually decorrelated to improve odor encoding in neural space (Friedrich and Laurent, 2001; Friedrich and Laurent, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Friedrich and Laurent, 2001 and Friedrich and Laurent, 2004.

claim: According to the Laurent model, temporal dynamics are not a necessary part of the odor code because they only facilitate coding optimization.
source: According to this model, temporal dynamics are not a necessary part of the odor code because they only facilitate coding optimization (Laurent, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Laurent, 2002.

claim: The odor representation becomes sparser and more decorrelated over time.
source: Support for this model comes from observations of temporally evolving neural dynamics and subsequent analyses demonstrating that the odor representation becomes sparser and more decorrelated over time (Friedrich and Laurent, 2004; Friedrich and Laurent, 2001; Gschwend et al., 2015; Gupta and Stopfer, 2014; Laurent et al., 1996; Wehr and Laurent, 1996)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Disturbing gamma oscillations impairs odor discrimination.
source: and that disturbing gamma oscillations impairs odor discrimination (Stopfer et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Stopfer et al., 1997.

claim: Most participants could hardly discriminate between TOMs composed of the same two components delivered in rapid succession in either one temporal order or its reverse.
source: We found that most participants could hardly discriminate between TOMs, although they easily discriminated between a TOM and one of its components.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Participants easily discriminated between a TOM and one of its components.
source: We found that most participants could hardly discriminate between TOMs, although they easily discriminated between a TOM and one of its components.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Participants succeeded in discriminating between the TOMs when they were notified of their successive nature in advance.
source: By contrast, participants succeeded in discriminating between the TOMs when they were notified of their successive nature in advance.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The time of glomerulus activation can be exploited to extract odor-related information, although it does not change the odor perception substantially.
source: We thus suggest that the time of glomerulus activation can be exploited to extract odor-related information, although it does not change the odor perception substantially, as should be expected from an odor code per se.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Out of the 10 participants who were tested with a time delay of 300 ms, nine failed to discriminate between the TOMs in a significant manner.
source: We observed that out of the 10 participants who were tested with a time delay of 300 ms, nine failed to discriminate between the TOMs in a significant manner; that is, their individual performance did not differ from chance (p>0.05, binomial test per participant).
evidence: This is a specific result from the experimental data.

claim: Group mean and median success rates for discriminating TOMs at Δt = 300 ms were close to chance levels (mean = 0.541, p=0.23; median = 0.55, p=0.51).
source: Group mean and median success rates were also close to chance levels (success rate: mean = 0.541, p=0.23, t-test; median = 0.55, p=0.51, two-sided sign test, N = 10, Figure 2A left violet panel).
evidence: This is a specific statistical result from the experimental data, also shown in Figure 2A.

claim: When using a longer interval of Δt = 600 ms between odor constituents, seven out of the nine participants (78% of the cohort) failed to discriminate significantly between the TOMs.
source: When we used a longer interval of Δt = 600 ms between odor constituents, seven out of the nine participants (78% of the cohort) failed to discriminate significantly between the TOMs.
evidence: This is a specific result from the experimental data.

claim: At Δt = 600 ms, there was only a slight improvement in group success rate (mean = 0.60, p=0.16; median = 0.5, p=1).
source: Overall, this resulted in only a slight improvement in group success rate (success rate: mean = 0.60, p=0.16, t-test; median = 0.5, p=1, two-sided sign test, N = 9, Figure 2A, left violet panel; Bayesian one sample t-test: BF10 = 1.626, error = 2.3E–4%).
evidence: This is a specific statistical result from the experimental data, also shown in Figure 2A.

claim: All participants except one could discriminate between the constituent odors when presented alone.
source: We found that all participants except one could discriminate between these odors (median success rate = 0.9 for A vs. (A / B). two-sided sign test p = 0.0156, Bayesian one sample t-test BF10 = 425.2, error = undetectable, N = 7; median success rate = 0.84 for B vs. (A / B), two-sided sign test: p = 0.0156, Bayesian one sample t-test BF10 = 121.9, error = undetectable, N = 7, Figure 2A, gray panel).
evidence: This is a specific result from the control experiments, also shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Most participants could discriminate between AB vs. (AB / AC) with median success rate = 0.75 (p = 0.004).
source: The findings showed that most participants could indeed discriminate between these odors (AB vs (AB / AC) (median success rate = 0.75; two-sided sign test, p = 0.004; Bayesian one sample t-test, BF10 = 219.4; error = undetectable; N = 9)
evidence: This is a specific result from the control experiments.

claim: Most participants could discriminate between AB vs. (AB / BC) with median success rate = 0.9 (p = 0.031).
source: and AB vs. (AB / BC) (median success rate = 0.9; two-sided sign test, p = 0.031; Bayesian one sample t-test, BF10 = 1031; error = undetectable; N = 6; Figure 2A gray panel, right plots)
evidence: This is a specific result from the control experiments, also shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The discrimination accuracies for TOMs tested with a delay of 300 or 600 ms were similar (p=0.89).
source: Planned post-hoc comparisons (corrected with Tukey HSD) revealed that the discrimination accuracies for TOMs tested with a delay of 300 or 600 ms were similar (p=0.89)
evidence: This is a specific statistical result from the ANOVA analysis.

claim: Performance in TOM discrimination was significantly lower than that in all control experiments, with the exception of one comparison between Δt = 600 ms and the control AB vs. (AB/AC), which was marginally significant (p=0.067).
source: and, more importantly, that performance in TOM discrimination was significantly lower than that in all control experiments, with the exception of one comparison between Δt = 600 ms and the control AB vs. (AB/AC), which was marginally significant (p=0.067).
evidence: This is a specific statistical result from the post-hoc comparisons.

claim: The majority of the cohort (~88% or 38 out of 43 participants) failed to discriminate significantly between the two TOMs composed of CTL and DMTS, regardless of the time delay.
source: In line with the previous experiment, the majority of the cohort (~88% or 38 out of 43 participants) failed to discriminate significantly between the two TOMs, regardless of the time delay (p>0.05, binomial test per each participant, uncorrected for multiple comparisons, Figure 3A left box).
evidence: This is a specific result from the experimental data, also shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The median for the group success rates was not significantly higher than chance for Δt = 75 and 150 ms and marginally significant for Δt = 300 and 600 ms.
source: The median for the group success rates was also not significantly higher than chance for Δt = 75 and 150 ms and marginally significant for Δt = 300 and 600 ms (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a specific statistical result from the experimental data, also shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Mean success rates per day in the extensive training experiment ranged from 0.51 to 0.64 and were not significantly different from chance.
source: Mean success rates per day ranged from 0.51 to 0.64 and were not significantly different from chance.
evidence: This is a specific result from the extensive training experiment.

claim: Success rates in the extensive training experiment did not improve as a function of session (two-sided sign test p>0.05 in 4 out of 5 sessions).
source: Critically, they did not improve as a function of session (two-sided sign test p>0.05 in 4 out of 5 sessions; note the marginal significance of cohort performance in the fourth session, p=0.0625, N = 4) (Figure 3B–C).
evidence: This is a specific statistical result from the extensive training experiment, also shown in Figure 3B-C.

claim: The two TOMs were perceived as an intermediate percept, positioned in space between the constituting two odor perceptions.
source: We observed that the two TOMs were perceived as an intermediate percept, positioned in space between the constituting two odor perceptions (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a finding from the odor rating experiment, shown in Figure 4A.

claim: While the two constituting odors were markedly different, the perceptual distance between the two TOMs was much smaller (Δt = 300 ms: distance A vs. B = 14.24 ± 4.09, AB vs. BA = 10.11 ± 3.48; t(286) = −9.21; Cohen's d = 1.08, p=7.35E–18).
source: Calculating the Euclidean distance between the average descriptor ratings of the four odor stimuli (e.g., A, B, AB, and BA for Δt = 300 and 600 ms) confirmed that while the two constituting odors were markedly different, the perceptual distance between the two TOMs was much smaller (Δt = 300 ms: distance (AU) A vs. B = 14.24 ± 4.09, AB vs. BA = 10.11 ± 3.48; two sample t-test, t(286) = −9.21; Cohen's d = 1.08, p=7.35E–18; Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a specific statistical result from the odor rating experiment, also shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The perceptual distance between the mono-molecules was larger than for all other stimuli (all p<0.0001).
source: Post-hoc comparisons confirmed that the perceptual distance between the mono-molecules was larger than for all other stimuli (all p<0.0001, Tukey HSD corrected) (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a specific statistical result from the post-hoc comparisons, also shown in Figure 4C.

claim: When the TOMs were delivered at a delay of 600 ms, the perceptual distance between the two TOMs remained distinctly smaller than the distance between their mono-molecular constituents (distance A vs. B = 18.86 ± 4.33, AB vs. BA = 10.98 ± 3.39; t(160) = −7.98; Cohen's d = 1.25, p=2.61E–13).
source: When the TOMs were delivered at a delay of 600 ms, a similar picture emerged in which the perceptual distance between the two TOMs remained distinctly smaller than the distance between their mono-molecular constituents (Figure 4D) (for Δt = 600 ms: Distance (AU) A vs. B = 18.86 ± 4.33, AB vs. BA = 10.98 ± 3.39; two sample t-test, t(160) = −7.98; Cohen's d = 1.25, p=2.61E–13; Figure 4E).
evidence: This is a specific statistical result from the odor rating experiment, also shown in Figure 4D and 4E.

claim: When participants were explicitly instructed that the incoming odor stimuli were composed of two consecutive odorants, there was an incremental improvement in both individual participants' success rates and the group's median performance.
source: In other words, when participants were explicitly instructed that the incoming odor stimuli were composed of two consecutive odorants, we observed an incremental improvement in both individual participants' success rates and the group's median performance.
evidence: This is a finding from the awareness experiment.

claim: For ORG/CIN, there was a significant main effect for 'Δt', implying that the success rate varied considerably as a function of the TOM Δt (F(3,44) = 6.05, partial eta-squared = 0.292, p=0.0015).
source: For ORG/CIN, we observed a significant main effect for 'Δt', implying that the success rate varied considerably as a function of the TOM Δt (F(3,44) = 6.05, partial eta-squared = 0.292, p=0.0015, N = 48, Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a specific statistical result from the ANOVA analysis, also shown in Figure 5A.

claim: For CTL/DMTS, there was a significant main effect for 'Δt' (F(3,28) = 19.94, partial eta-squared = 0.681, p<0.00001).
source: A parallel analysis conducted on the CTL/DMTS odorant pair indicated a similar significant main effect for 'Δt' (F(3,28) = 19.94, partial eta-squared = 0.681, p<0.00001, N = 36, Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a specific statistical result from the ANOVA analysis, also shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Glomeruli activation times do not elicit a prominent difference in odor percept.
source: Thus, overall, glomeruli activation times do not elicit a prominent difference in odor percept; however, they can be used to extract temporal odor information such as detecting the order of odor delivery in a sequence.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Glomeruli activation times can be used to extract temporal odor information such as detecting the order of odor delivery in a sequence.
source: Thus, overall, glomeruli activation times do not elicit a prominent difference in odor percept; however, they can be used to extract temporal odor information such as detecting the order of odor delivery in a sequence.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: The results are more consistent with one possible interpretation of the Laurent model — that time is not necessarily part of the code — and less so with the Hopfield model that time is part of the code.
source: We view these results as more consistent with one possible interpretation of the Laurent model — that time is not necessarily part of the code — and less so with the Hopfield model that time is part of the code.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results in the context of existing models.

claim: The results do not align with a temporal coding model in which the first activated glomeruli form the odor code.
source: Moreover, the results do not align with a temporal coding model in which the first activated glomeruli form the odor code (Schaefer and Margrie, 2007; Wilson et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results in the context of existing models.

claim: Although the latency code only weakly affects the odor percept of the TOM, it could be used to disentangle the constituent odors, provided that the sequential nature of the stimuli is disclosed, and the temporal dynamics do not evolve too rapidly.
source: This may suggest that although the latency code only weakly affects the odor percept of the TOM, it could be used to disentangle the constituent odors, provided that the sequential nature of the stimuli is disclosed, and the temporal dynamics do not evolve too rapidly.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results from the awareness experiment.

claim: When a delay was introduced, there was a substantial duration of time in which there was no odor at all, and this pause between the two odors might have been used to detect the existence of two odors.
source: One possible interpretation of this result is that when a delay was introduced, there was a substantial duration of time in which there was no odor at all. This pause between the two odors might have been used to detect the existence of two odors and might therefore have contributed to perceiving them as two odors delivered one after the other.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental results.

claim: Participants may have employed a pattern-matching algorithm, actively searching for a specific odor to occur at the beginning or end of the stimulus.
source: Another possible explanation is that participants performed well because they employed a pattern-matching algorithm. A few participants reported that they were actively searching for a specific odor to occur at the beginning or end of the stimulus, suggesting that they employed a matching algorithm for one of the constituents.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on participant reports.

claim: When the delay was set to be shorter than 150 ms, pattern matching failed because the first odor was presented in a partial temporal overlap with the second one.
source: When the delay was set to be shorter than 150 ms, this matching failed because the first odor was presented in a partial temporal overlap with the second one.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental results and participant reports.

claim: Glomeruli activation time can be utilized to extract odor-related information such as when the odor was delivered relative to other odors or relative to respiration phase.
source: These results thus suggest that glomeruli activation time can be utilized to extract odor-related information such as when the odor was delivered relative to other odors or relative to respiration phase.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: In mascrosmatic animals who rely more heavily on their sense of smell, such as rodents and insects, temporal coding may be part of the odor code.
source: One can speculate that in mascrosmatic animals who rely more heavily on their sense of smell, such as rodents and insects, temporal coding is part of the odor code.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about other species.

claim: Mice learned to discriminate between two light stimulations of the OSNs, M/Ts or even a single glomerulus that were a few milliseconds apart, either relative to, or irrespective of respiration.
source: Mice learned to discriminate between two light stimulations of the OSNs, M/Ts or even a single glomerulus that were a few milliseconds apart, either relative to, or irrespective of respiration (Rebello et al., 2014; Smear et al., 2011; Smear et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Rebello et al., 2014; Smear et al., 2011; Smear et al., 2013.

claim: The optogenetic experiments in mice clearly demonstrated the use of timing in the olfactory system of mice, but did not demonstrate that mice perceived the optogenetic stimulations as two different odor percepts.
source: These experiments clearly demonstrated the use of timing in the olfactory system of mice. However, they did not demonstrate that mice perceived the optogenetic stimulations as two different odor percepts as mice cannot report their odor perception directly.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the cited studies.

claim: The trained mice may have perceived the two optogenetic stimuli as the same odor presented at different respiration phases.
source: One possible interpretation is that the trained mice perceived the two optogenetic stimuli as the same odor presented at different respiration phases.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the cited studies.

claim: The mice may have perceived the optogenetic stimuli as two different 'odor' durations or two odors delivered one after the other.
source: Alternatively, the mice may have perceived the optogenetic stimuli as two different 'odor' durations or two odors delivered one after the other.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the cited studies.

claim: Although latency coding does not substantially affect odor perception, temporal dynamics can be utilized under extreme conditions.
source: It is thus possible that although latency coding does not substantially affect odor perception, temporal dynamics can be utilized under extreme conditions.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the experimental findings and literature review.

claim: A substantial amount of odor information can be extracted from 'sub-sniff' neuron spike timings.
source: Several studies have shown that a substantial amount of odor information can be extracted from 'sub-sniff' neuron spike timings (Bathellier et al., 2008; Bolding and Franks, 2017; Cury and Uchida, 2010; Sirotin et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Whether the temporal dynamics observed in odor-elicited neural responses in rodents are part of the odor code remains an ongoing debate.
source: Thus, overall, whether the temporal dynamics observed in odor-elicited neural responses in rodents are part of the odor code remains an ongoing debate.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of the field.

claim: Experiments in humans indicate that latency coding could be utilized to extract odor-related information without substantially affecting odor perception.
source: Our experiments in humans indicate that latency coding could be utilized to extract odor-related information without substantially affecting odor perception.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: The average latency of the PID-reported odor signal onset was within the range of 20–40 ms.
source: The average latency of the PID-reported odor signal onset was within the range of 20–40 ms, and the odor concentration returned to 10% of its peak value within 30–50 ms after odor offset (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is a measurement from the PID validation experiments, shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B.

claim: The odor concentration returned to 10% of its peak value within 30–50 ms after odor offset.
source: The average latency of the PID-reported odor signal onset was within the range of 20–40 ms, and the odor concentration returned to 10% of its peak value within 30–50 ms after odor offset (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is a measurement from the PID validation experiments, shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B.

claim: Switching the order of the odors in the TOM will create a substantial difference in the glomerular activation times, because the glomerular activation times of two odors in the first TOM were shifted by +Δt and by –Δt in the second TOM.
source: That said, even assuming some delay in glomerulus activation due to these interactions, switching the order of the odors in the TOM will nevertheless create a substantial difference in the glomerular activation times, because the glomerular activation times of two odors in the first TOM were shifted by +Δt and by –Δt in the second TOM.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the experimental design.

claim: An inter-stimulus-interval (ISI) of 8 s was used between the two TOMs because when ISI was longer, performance was significantly hampered even when the participants were asked to discriminate between the two constituent odors.
source: We used an inter-stimulus-interval (ISI) of 8 s between the two TOMs rather than the more common 10–20 s interval employed in human olfaction experimentation, because we observed in pilot sessions that when ISI was longer, performance was significantly hampered even when the participants were asked to discriminate between the two constituent odors (i.e., odor A vs. odor B).
evidence: This is a methodological decision based on pilot data.

claim: The task essentially became an olfactory match-to-sample working memory task rather than a discrimination task when ISI was longer, which is more difficult as the ISI gets longer.
source: This was probably due to the fact that the task essentially became an olfactory match-to-sample working memory task rather than a discrimination task, which is more difficult as the ISI gets longer (Arzi et al., 2014; Zelano et al., 2009).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citations to Arzi et al., 2014 and Zelano et al., 2009.

claim: Each participant conducted a maximum of 20 trials to minimize sensory fatigue resulting from repeated odor exposure.
source: To minimize sensory fatigue resulting from repeated odor exposure, each participant conducted a maximum of 20 trials (i.e., 20 × 2 = 40 odor trials), which is within the range used in olfaction psychophysics experiments (Johnson et al., 2003; Weiss et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a methodological decision supported by citations to Johnson et al., 2003 and Weiss et al., 2012.

claim: There was no significant difference in perceived intensity between ORG and CIN (ORG = 3.89 ± 0.12, CIN = 4.14 ± 0.15, paired t-test: t(10) = –0.45, p = 0.66, Cohen's d = –1.76).
source: There was no significant difference in intensity (perceived intensity: ORG = 3.89 ± 0.12, CIN = 4.14 ± 0.15, paired t-test: t(10) = –0.45, p = 0.66, Cohen's d = –1.76, Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a specific statistical result from the intensity rating experiment, shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Participants made a similar number of wrong answers in trials in which the second TOM was the same as the first ('Same') or different ('Diff.') (Same = 0.505 ± 0.028, Diff = 0.495 ± 0.011, paired t-test: t(9) = 0.11, p=0.92, Cohen's d = 0.45).
source: Participants made a similar number of wrong answers in trials in which the second TOM was the same as the first ('Same') or different ('Diff.'). This suggests that neither condition was easier than the other and that there was no strong bias in the participants' report towards one answer over the other (analysis for Δt = 300 ms: Same = 0.505 ± 0.028, Diff = 0.495 ± 0.011, paired t-test: t(9) = 0.11, p=0.92, Cohen's d = 0.45, Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a specific statistical result from the experimental data, shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The perceptual distance between CTL and DMTS was significantly higher than the distance between ORG and CIN (CTL/DMTS = 5.52 ± 1.12; CIN/ORG = 4.18 ± 1.25, paired t test: t(110) = 5.95, p=3.1E–8, Cohen's d = 1.12).
source: The perceptual distance between CTL and DMTS was significantly higher than the distance between ORG and CIN (CTL/DMTS = 5.52 ± 1.12; CIN/ORG = 4.18 ± 1.25, paired t test: t(110) = 5.95, p=3.1E–8, Cohen's d = 1.12, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a specific statistical result from the odor similarity analysis, shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: There was no significant difference in perceived intensity between CTL and DMTS (CTL = 7.37 ± 1.19, DMTS = 7.12 ± 0.99, paired t-test, t(7) = −0.84, Cohen's d = 0.23, p=0.43).
source: Last, as with the previous TOMs, we verified that these two odors had similar intensities (CTL = 7.37 ± 1.19, DMTS = 7.12 ± 0.99, paired t-test, t(7) = −0.84, Cohen's d = 0.23, p=0.43, N = 8).
evidence: This is a specific statistical result from the intensity rating experiment.

claim: The respiratory phases for the first and second TOMs were correlated, both for correct and incorrect trials (correct: circular correlation r = 0.67, p=1.33E-8; incorrect: r = 0.549, p=1.02E-5).
source: The respiration phases for the first and second TOMs were correlated, both for correct and incorrect trials (correct: circular correlation r = 0.67, p=1.33E-8, N = 100; incorrect: r = 0.549, p=1.02E-5, N = 84).
evidence: This is a specific statistical result from the respiratory phase analysis.

claim: The phase differences in the correct and incorrect trials were not significantly different (Kruskal-Wallis test for circular data: shared population median = −0.478 rad, KW(P)=1.402, p=0.236).
source: Moreover, comparing the differences between the TOMs' respiration phases (e.g., TOM1 – TOM2) in correct and incorrect trials further showed that the phase differences in the correct and incorrect trials were not significantly different (non-parametric multi-sample test for equal medians, Kruskal-Wallis test for circular data: shared population median = −0.478 rad, KW(P)=1.402, p=0.236; Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–D).
evidence: This is a specific statistical result from the respiratory phase analysis, shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–D.

claim: 73 participants were excluded from analysis following trial-by-trial data review, leaving a total of 284 participants.
source: This led to the exclusion of 73 participants following analysis of their trial-by-trial data, leaving a total of 284 participants.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about participant exclusion.

claim: The number of eliminated trials within the pool of remaining participants who took part in the TOM paradigms totaled 162 out of 1940 (8.3%) for CIN/ORG and 223 out of 3972 (5.6%) for CTL/DMTS experiments.
source: The number of eliminated trials within the pool of remaining participants who took part in the TOM paradigms totaled 162 out of 1940 and 223 out of 3972 trials, or 8.3% and 5.6% of all events in the CIN/ORG and CTL/DMTS experiments, respectively.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about trial exclusion.

claim: The temporal odor mixtures (TOMs) were comprised of fragrant oil mixtures of orange (ORG) and cinnamon (CIN), or of the monomolecular odorants Citral (CTL) and Dimethyl Trisulfide (DMTS).
source: The temporal odor mixtures (TOMs) were comprised of fragrant oil mixtures of orange (ORG) and cinnamon (CIN), or of the monomolecular odorants Citral (CTL) (CAS: 5392-40-5, Sigma-Aldrich) and Dimethyl Trisulfide (DMTS) (CAS: 3658-80-8, Sigma Aldrich).
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the experimental stimuli.

claim: Odors were diluted to equally perceived intensity (CTL: 1:100, ORG: 1:1, DMTS, 1:10000, CIN: 1:1).
source: In both cases, odors were diluted to equally perceived intensity (CTL: 1:100, ORG: 1:1, DMTS, 1:10000, CIN: 1:1).
evidence: This is a methodological detail about odor preparation.

claim: The main constituents of cinnamon oil according to their relative contribution to the mixture were E-cinnamaldehyde, linalool, o-cymene, terpineol and cinnamyl acetate.
source: Cinnamon oil: E-cinnamaldehyde (CAS 14371-10-9), linalool (CAS 78-70-6), o-cymene (CAS 527-84-4), terpineol (CAS 98-55-5) and cinnamyl acetate (CAS 103-54-8).
evidence: This is a result from the GCMS analysis of the odor composition.

claim: The main constituents of orange oil according to their relative contribution to the mixture were limonene, gardenol and linalool.
source: Orange oil: limonene (CAS 138-86-3), gardenol (CAS 93-92-5) and linalool (CAS 78-70-9).
evidence: This is a result from the GCMS analysis of the odor composition.

claim: A computer-controlled air-dilution custom-built olfactometer was used to deliver odors in varying orders and sequence lengths.
source: We used a computer-controlled air-dilution custom-built olfactometer to deliver odors in varying orders and sequence lengths.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the experimental apparatus.

claim: Odor stimuli lasted 200 ms.
source: Odor stimuli lasted 200 ms.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the experimental parameters.

claim: The inter-stimulus interval (i.e., the time between two TOMs) was set to 8 s.
source: The inter-stimulus interval (i.e., the time between two TOMs) was set to 8 s.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the experimental parameters.

claim: The next trial was presented 23 s after the participant submitted his or her answer.
source: The next trial (i.e., the next pair of TOMs) was presented 23 s after the participant submitted his or her answer (which usually lasted ~2–5 s).
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the experimental parameters.

claim: Nasal respiration was recorded using a nasal cannula attached to a pressure-sensitive transducer.
source: Nasal respiration was recorded using a nasal cannula attached to a pressure-sensitive transducer, which translated these changes in pressure into an electrical signal via a USB interface (Plotkin et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the experimental apparatus, supported by a citation to Plotkin et al., 2010.

claim: The signal was acquired and digitized at a sampling rate of 1 KHz.
source: The signal was acquired and digitized at a sampling rate of 1 KHz.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about data acquisition.

claim: Purified air (medical grade 99.999%) was used to deliver odors.
source: To deliver an odor, purified air (medical grade 99.999%, Maxima, Israel) was streamed through a glass vial containing a liquid odor.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the experimental apparatus.

claim: The air flow was set to 1.8 LPM using a mass flow controller.
source: The air flow was set to 1.8 LPM using a mass flow controller (Alicat Scientific).
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the experimental parameters.

claim: Odors and the odor-delivery plastic tubing were replaced every day.
source: Odors and the odor-delivery plastic tubing were replaced every day.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about experimental procedures.

claim: Participants were seated approximately 5 cm from the odor ports.
source: To prevent contamination, participants were seated in front of three dedicated odor ports, one for each of the odorants (the distance from the odor ports was ~5 cm, Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the experimental setup, shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Trials in which the odor presentation extended into the exhalation period or started prematurely before inhalation were excluded from the analysis.
source: Trials in which the odor presentation extended into the exhalation period or started prematurely before inhalation were excluded from the analysis (Figure 1F, methods).
evidence: This is a methodological detail about data analysis, shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The delay between the two odors, Δt, was set to ≤600 ms.
source: The delay between the two odors, Δt, was set to ≤600 ms.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the experimental parameters.

claim: Longer delays were not tested because the overall duration of a TOM had to be shorter than a typical inhalation period (about 1–1.5 s) to be perceived in full and to minimize the possibility of discriminating between the two TOMs by realizing that they were composed of two consecutive odors.
source: We did not test longer delays because the overall duration of a TOM had to be shorter than a typical inhalation period (about 1–1.5 s) to be perceived in full and to minimize the possibility of discriminating between the two TOMs by realizing that they were composed of two consecutive odors.
evidence: This is a methodological justification for the experimental design.

claim: At long delays (e.g., 300 and 600 ms) a few participants realized that the TOMs were composed of two consecutive odors.
source: In fact, at long delays (e.g., 300 and 600 ms) a few participants realized that the TOMs were composed of two consecutive odors.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: Participants who realized that the TOMs were composed of two consecutive odors were not excluded from the analysis to prevent bias.
source: We did not exclude these participants from our analysis to prevent bias.
evidence: This is a methodological decision about data analysis.

claim: All TOMs elicited similar response dynamics as measured by PID.
source: All TOMs elicited similar response dynamics.
evidence: This is a result from the PID validation experiments.

claim: PID responses varied between different delays and the order of odor presentation, reflecting the between-odor interactions and inter-pipe flow interactions.
source: PID responses varied between these delays and the order of odor presentation, reflecting the between-odor interactions and inter-pipe flow interactions.
evidence: This is a result from the PID validation experiments.

claim: The odor concentration of the odor constituents and the TOMs in three tested delays was highly similar across trials of the same condition.
source: However, the odor concentration of the odor constituents and the TOMs in three tested delays was highly similar across trials of the same condition.
evidence: This is a result from the PID validation experiments.

claim: Each TOM was expected to elicit the same odor percept across all trials.
source: Thus, each TOM was expected to elicit the same odor percept across all trials.
evidence: This is an inference based on the PID measurements.

claim: The order of odor presentation was preserved when placing the PID inlet ~5 cm from the odor ports.
source: Measurements of odor concentration when placing the PID inlet ~5 cm from the odor ports (i.e., the location of the participants' nose) revealed that the order of odor presentation was preserved, although the odor concentration was more variable across trials when measured at a 5 cm distance (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a result from the PID validation experiments, shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The odor concentration was more variable across trials when measured at a 5 cm distance.
source: Measurements of odor concentration when placing the PID inlet ~5 cm from the odor ports (i.e., the location of the participants' nose) revealed that the order of odor presentation was preserved, although the odor concentration was more variable across trials when measured at a 5 cm distance (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a result from the PID validation experiments, shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Any participant with a total number of fewer than 14 valid trials (70% of the session) was excluded from further analysis.
source: Any participant with a total number of fewer than 14 valid trials (70% of the session) was excluded from further analysis.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about participant exclusion criteria.

claim: The results remained the same when using a less stringent cut-off for trial exclusion or when assuming a very long odor offset of 200 ms.
source: The results remained the same when we used a less stringent cut-off (e.g., 0.9) or when we assumed that odor offset was longer than the estimate obtained from the PID measurements (e.g., assuming a very long odor offset of 200 ms).
evidence: This is a result from sensitivity analyses of the data.

claim: A success rate significantly higher than chance in a 20-trial experiment was calculated to be 0.70 (binomial cumulative distribution function).
source: A success rate significantly higher than chance in a 20-trial experiment was therefore calculated to be 0.70 (binomial cumulative distribution function).
evidence: This is a statistical calculation for determining significance.

claim: Odorants and TOMs were rated using a set of eleven verbal descriptors (pleasant, fruity, edible, hot, chemical, medicinal, smoky, alcoholic, attractive, earthy, and sulfurous) on a scale ranging from 0 to 10.
source: Odorant and TOMs were rated using a set of eleven verbal descriptors (pleasant, fruity, edible, hot, chemical, medicinal, smoky, alcoholic, attractive, earthy, and sulfurous) on a scale of ranging from 0 to 10 (where 0 corresponded to 'not at all' and 10 corresponded to 'very much').
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the odor rating procedure.

claim: In rating sessions involving TOMs, these were always rated before the monomolecular odors in order to prevent bias in the perception of the mixtures.
source: It should be noted that in rating sessions involving TOMs, these were always rated before the monomolecular odors in order to prevent bias in the perception of the mixtures, given that their isolated components had not yet been presented separately.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the experimental procedure to prevent bias.

claim: Participants could undergo several smelling rounds of the same odor before rating.
source: Participants could undergo several smelling rounds of the same odor before rating, and an inter-stimulus interval of 23 s was imposed between any two odor presentations.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the rating procedure.

claim: An inter-stimulus interval of 23 s was imposed between any two odor presentations during rating sessions.
source: Participants could undergo several smelling rounds of the same odor before rating, and an inter-stimulus interval of 23 s was imposed between any two odor presentations.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the rating procedure.

source: The experiment was approved by the institutional ethics committee of Bar Ilan University (reference number ISU20140804001).
evidence: This is a statement about ethical approval.

source: Written informed consent and consent to publish was obtained from the participants in accordance with the ethical standards of the Declaration of Helsinki (1964).

source: This manuscript describes a series of experiments conducted on an overall cohort of 284 participants (191 female, 93 male, age range 18–41 years).
